title: Fake SpaceX Stock Isn’t Worth as Much

preschool.title: The Rocket Shares in the Locked Box
preschool.lesson: If you buy something through a middleman, you need a way to check that the middleman really owns it.
paragraphs: Some people wanted to own a little piece of SpaceX before its stock could be freely traded.
So they gave money to special little companies that said, ‘We own SpaceX shares for you.’
For a while, the real shares were locked up and could not be handed over. Investors mostly had statements saying what they owned.
When the lock finally opened, some people could ask, ‘Okay, may I have my shares now?’ That is when a pretend promise becomes much harder to hide.

elementary.title: When the Lockup Opens: The Case of the Phantom SpaceX Shares
elementary.lesson: An SPV (special purpose vehicle) is supposed to own underlying private-company shares and give investors pro rata ownership, but transfer restrictions and opaque recordkeeping can let SPV promoters claim or sell more shares than they actually hold, leaving investors with only account statements rather than registered shares.
paragraphs: In a little online box called an SPV, people bought a piece of SpaceX's sky,
They paid a sum, they  clicked "confirm," they trusted the numbers on the fly.
Ram Rupireddy wired in his money — $17,250 was sent along,
Late Stage Management said they held the stock; the portal sang the same old song.
Back then he thought SpaceX was worth about $58 billion on the sheet,
Then June arrived and SpaceX leapt to $1.77 trillion — a carnival feat.
Ram saw his portal list 2,500 shares, a number he took as true,
At the IPO price he guessed that that meant more than $300,000 in view.
But Late Stage later emailed, saying the SPV sold shares in 2024,
At around $105 each (that was before a 5-1 stock split they swore).
So the firm said his holding then was worth $45,450 — a very different song,
And the portal and the tax form and the story did not easily belong.
SPVs can own real stock, or just the paper that pretends to be,
Promoters could spend on yachts while account statements promise the sea.
There are at least a thousand SpaceX-tied SPVs, bankers say,
And when the lockup opens — that’s the test — investors will ask for shares that day.
Some will get rocket stock in hand, some will get cash for what was sold,
Some might find their login dead, the answers curt, the portal cold.
True or fake, the muddle proves how trust can bend and sometimes break,
And now the market tide has gone out — we’ll see who’s been truly awake.

What happened? A special purpose vehicle (SPV) sold interests that purported to give investors pro rata ownership of SpaceX shares, but because private-company shares were transfer-restricted and the SPV kept only account statements, investors could not confirm registered ownership; when SpaceX IPO’d at a $1.77 trillion valuation, Late Stage Management told Ram Rupireddy that the SPV had sold the SpaceX shares in 2024 at about $105 each (pre 5-1 split), leaving his holding valued at $45,450, while his investor portal and tax form had indicated an equivalent of 2,500 shares worth over $300,000 at the IPO price.

middle.title: The Lockup Becomes an Audit
middle.lesson: Illiquid assets create verification risk because investors may have only an intermediary’s records until the assets can actually be transferred.
paragraphs: SPVs let investors get indirect exposure to private companies such as SpaceX. The structure is simple in theory: the vehicle owns a fixed number of company shares, and investors own proportional interests in the vehicle.

The weakness is verification. A dishonest promoter could fail to buy the shares at all, or sell claims on more shares than the SPV owns. While the underlying stock is private and transfer-restricted, investors may have little beyond the promoter’s statements and ledgers.

SpaceX’s IPO and subsequent lockup expiration change that. Once the underlying shares can be distributed or sold, investors can demand delivery or cash. A long period of unverifiable bookkeeping suddenly meets a hard settlement test.

That is why a successful company can expose fraud rather than conceal it: soaring values encourage investors to ask for their supposed winnings. Matt Levine’s joke is that the tide does not always reveal the fraud when markets crash; sometimes the problem appears when everyone tries to collect the fabulous profits.

high.title: SPVs, Transferability and the Bezzle
high.lesson: When an investment is difficult to transfer, intermediary records can substitute for settlement for years; a liquidity event turns that soft claim into a hard test.
paragraphs: A private-company SPV separates beneficial ownership from the issuer’s shareholder ledger. Investors own interests in the vehicle, while the vehicle is supposed to own the underlying SpaceX shares. That creates two obvious fraud opportunities: the vehicle may not own the stated shares, or it may issue more economic claims than its actual position can support.

Transfer restrictions make those claims unusually difficult to verify. Before an IPO—and often during a post-IPO lockup—an investor cannot simply demand delivery into a brokerage account. The promoter’s statement can therefore function as the evidence of ownership even when the evidence is wrong.

SpaceX’s lockup release converts that information problem into a settlement problem. Investors can ask for their pro-rata shares or sale proceeds. A legitimate SPV can perform; an over-issued or fictitious one cannot.

This is a version of the ‘bezzle’: the period when both the investor and the fraudster can feel as though the money exists. A rising asset price can actually shorten that period because investors become eager to realize gains. The better SpaceX performs, the more urgently everyone wants the very shares that may never have been there.

preschool.title: Borrowing Money to Buy More of the Same Thing
preschool.lesson: A loan can use an investment as collateral, but if that investment falls in value the borrower may need to add more money.
paragraphs: SoftBank owned a very valuable investment in OpenAI.
A group of banks said, ‘We will lend you money because you can promise those OpenAI shares as backup.’
SoftBank borrowed a lot of money—and planned to use that money to buy even more OpenAI.
So the pile of OpenAI helped pay for a bigger pile of OpenAI.

elementary.title: Borrowing Against OpenAI to Buy More OpenAI
elementary.lesson: SoftBank Group used its OpenAI stake to borrow $10 billion from banks, and will pay another $10 billion by October as the final part of a $30 billion investment. The loan is a margin loan requiring SoftBank to inject cash if its valuation falls; OpenAI shares are not publicly traded, so pricing is harder.
paragraphs: A company called SoftBank had a share, a bright and shiny part of OpenAI’s heart.
They loved the idea of owning more, so they knocked upon the bankers’ door.
The banks said, “We’ll lend you cash, ten billion dollars we’ll stash.”
SoftBank smiled and took the loan, and put its OpenAI stake up as a stone.
The money's for buying more of the same: another ten billion is the next claim,
It’s the last piece of a thirty-billion plan, due by October—buy more if you can.
Banks usually lend against stocks you can see; public prices tell them what things be.
But OpenAI’s shares are private, not on a public street—the price is hidden, so the risk is steep.
In normal margin loans you must add cash if prices dip, or the lender can seize what’s on the ship.
SoftBank agreed that if its value should fall, it would add cash so the banks won’t stall.
So many people in finance now joke and groan, “Borrowing against OpenAI to buy more OpenAI” — that’s grown
into a funny, risky loop where the same thing funds itself, and a small wobble could hurt many on the shelf.
Other firms, like Anthropic, sit in a similar crowd; lenders build big deals and sometimes speak aloud
about data-center bonds and pledges to pay for compute, turning future deals into today’s money to route.
If the valuation collapses, banks that lent this cash will be in trouble fast — and so will many more in the cast.
This all shows how a single bet can stretch and bend: one loan, another buy, and the risk can spread to no end.

What happened? SoftBank Group used its stake in OpenAI as collateral to borrow $10 billion from banks and plans to pay another $10 billion by October as the final part of a $30 billion investment. The loan is a margin loan that requires SoftBank to inject additional cash if its valuation falls, and OpenAI’s shares are not publicly traded so pricing is harder.

middle.title: A $10 Billion Private-Stock Margin Loan
middle.lesson: Collateral can turn equity value into borrowing capacity, but concentrated borrowing magnifies exposure when the collateral and the new investment are the same asset.
paragraphs: SoftBank borrowed $10 billion from a bank group against its OpenAI stake while preparing to invest another $10 billion in OpenAI, part of a roughly $30 billion commitment.

That is a margin loan: the borrower pledges shares as collateral and may have to add cash if their value falls. The unusual part is that OpenAI is private and unprofitable, so lenders cannot continuously observe a public market price or easily sell the collateral.

The transaction fits a broader AI-finance pattern. Data-center loans and other structures increasingly rely, directly or indirectly, on the enormous market-implied value of OpenAI and Anthropic. Equity valuations are becoming raw material for debt.

SoftBank’s trade is therefore both simple and concentrated: turn OpenAI equity into cash, then turn the cash back into OpenAI equity. The same thesis supports the collateral, the borrowing capacity and the new purchase.

high.title: Equity Value as Debt Capacity
high.lesson: A private-company margin loan monetizes equity value without selling it, but valuation opacity and correlated collateral make the leverage unusually reflexive.
paragraphs: SoftBank’s $10 billion loan against its OpenAI stake is economically familiar—a margin loan—but unusual in scale and collateral. Public-stock margin lending relies on observable prices and liquid collateral; OpenAI is private, loss-making and not continuously marked by a market.

The facility nevertheless includes a requirement for SoftBank to inject additional cash if OpenAI’s valuation declines. That means the banks have effectively underwritten both a valuation methodology and SoftBank’s ability to meet a future collateral call.

The larger point is that enormous AI equity valuations are increasingly functioning as debt capacity even when the companies themselves have little traditional corporate debt. Data-center obligations, guarantees and now direct loans against equity all translate expected future AI cash flows into present financing.

The reflexivity is obvious: SoftBank pledges OpenAI to borrow $10 billion and uses the proceeds to buy more OpenAI. A rising valuation supports more borrowing; a falling valuation weakens the collateral while simultaneously impairing the asset purchased with the loan.

preschool.title: The One-Penny Toll
preschool.lesson: A penny fee feels tiny on a big trade and much bigger on a fifty-cent trade.
paragraphs: Imagine two roads that both charge a one-penny toll.
One road carries something worth about $100. The penny is almost nothing.
The other road carries something worth about 50 cents. Now the same penny is a much bigger bite.
That helps explain why little prediction-market contracts can be surprisingly profitable to trade.

elementary.title: Why a Penny Is Huge in Prediction Markets
elementary.lesson: The same one-cent trading increment can be tiny for a stock and enormous for a fifty-cent prediction contract.
paragraphs: Prediction-market contracts are tiny. A typical contract pays either $1 or $0, and across Yes and No contracts the average price is roughly 50 cents.
But prices usually move in one-cent steps.
One cent on a 50-cent contract is 2%. That is a pretty chunky step.
Stocks also commonly move in one-cent steps, but a normal stock might cost around $100 or $150. One cent compared with $150 is almost invisible.
This matters because the gap between what buyers pay and sellers receive—the bid-ask spread—is where market makers and brokers can earn money.

Robinhood reported that customers traded about $956 billion of stocks and 13.6 billion event contracts. Yet Robinhood made $129 million of transaction revenue from stocks and $156 million from event contracts.
So a much smaller pile of prediction-market trading produced more transaction revenue than the enormous pile of stock trading.
Matt Levine’s wonderfully small explanation is: pennies are much bigger when the thing itself costs only fifty cents.

middle.title: Prediction Markets Have Giant Pennies
middle.lesson: Tick size relative to notional value helps explain why prediction-market volume can be unusually lucrative for intermediaries.
paragraphs: A binary event contract pays $1 or $0 and has an average price around $0.50. With a minimum price increment of $0.01, one tick is roughly 2% of the contract’s value.
For a stock priced around $150, the same one-cent tick is only about 0.007%. That gives market makers much more economic room per dollar traded in event contracts.

Robinhood’s results illustrate the point. Customers traded vastly more stock value than event-contract value, yet event contracts generated more transaction-based revenue: about $156 million versus $129 million for stocks.

There are other differences between the businesses, but relative tick size gives a simple reason brokers and market makers are enthusiastic about prediction markets: a penny-wide economics can be enormous when the underlying instrument is tiny.

high.title: Tick Size Is Market Structure
high.lesson: Minimum price increments set a floor under spread economics, so identical nominal ticks can produce radically different intermediation rents across asset classes.
paragraphs: Binary event contracts have $1 terminal notional and an average trading price near $0.50. A $0.01 tick is therefore roughly 200 basis points of price. For a $150 equity, the same penny is less than one basis point.

A coarse tick can keep quoted spreads wider than pure competition might otherwise produce, creating more economic surplus for liquidity providers and brokers. Decimalization did the reverse for equities by shrinking spreads dramatically.

Robinhood’s reported economics are striking: roughly $956 billion of stock trading generated about $129 million of transaction revenue, while 13.6 billion event contracts generated about $156 million. Levine approximates the broker’s take as one penny per $100 stock trade versus one penny per $1 event contract.

The comparison is deliberately simplified, but it captures an important market-structure point: product design determines the unit in which competition occurs, and that unit can determine how much revenue intermediaries can extract from apparently similar trading activity.

preschool.title: The Investor Who Got Right Back Up
preschool.lesson: A good idea can still go badly if you borrow too much money to pursue it.
paragraphs: Leopold liked investing in artificial-intelligence companies very, very much.
His hedge fund borrowed lots of money, and lenders demanded it back when markets moved against him.
That nearly wrecked the fund.
A few days later, he was investing in AI again—this time without giving up on the big idea just because the risky borrowing had gone wrong.

elementary.title: Leo’s Fast, Loud Leap
elementary.lesson: Long rhyming picture-book about the real events: margin calls, Citadel seizing public assets, $400 million into a private company, and his decision about leverage.
paragraphs: He watched the light on his screen and said, "AI is coming fast," with eyes that shone like chrome,
But bets that stretch on borrowed cash can topple towers made of foam.
He ran a hedge fund called Situational Awareness, proud and bold and clever,
A long/short book, a plan with 5x leverage — a ladder that might not hold forever.
One morning papers fluttered in: margin calls, the lenders calling loud,
Citadel and others wanted cash; his public holdings lost their crowd.
His portfolio’s edges were pulled into the maw of jaws that seize and bind,
Tens of billions, we are told, went misty in the wind left behind.
Most people might unpack their bags and find a quiet, gentle place to rest,
But Leo, fresh from vows and rings, put cash into a different quest.
He plunked down four hundred million — $400,000,000 — into a company not on any public floor,
A private bet on AI’s quickness, because he said the future’s knocking at the door.
Some called it brash, some called it brave; the picture tasted oddly sweet:
He’d learned to cut the borrowed rope, he’d slow the leverage of his feet.
Yet still he liked his venture route, where startups bloom out of a seed,
So he stopped the borrowed cliff and kept the pace he thought they need.

What happened? Aschenbrenner’s hedge fund Situational Awareness ran a long/short portfolio at about 5x gross leverage and faced margin calls from lenders, including actions that let Citadel take down much of his public positions. Days after those margin calls, he invested $400,000,000 into a privately held company and said he would stop using leverage but continue investing in private AI opportunities.

middle.title: Right Thesis, Wrong Funding
middle.lesson: Investment selection and capital structure are separate decisions: a long-run thesis can be sound while leverage makes the portfolio unable to survive short-run volatility.
paragraphs: Leopold Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness was built around a bullish AI thesis, but its public hedge-fund portfolio used substantial leverage. When prices moved against it, margin calls forced a crisis and much of the portfolio was transferred to Citadel.
That failure does not logically disprove the underlying AI thesis. It shows a maturity mismatch: a long-horizon conviction was financed with borrowing that could be called on a short horizon.

Days later, Aschenbrenner reportedly invested $400 million in a private company, signaling that he had not abandoned the AI view. He also got married over the weekend, which gives the story its absurd velocity.

The cleaner version of the strategy is therefore not ‘stop believing in AI’; it is ‘do not finance a volatile, long-duration thesis with leverage that can force liquidation before the thesis has time to play out.’

high.title: Duration Mismatch in an AI Hedge Fund
high.lesson: Leverage can transform a long-duration investment thesis into a short-duration solvency problem.
paragraphs: Situational Awareness’s near-collapse illustrates the difference between asset risk and funding risk. Aschenbrenner’s thesis was that AI assets would compound dramatically over time; the hedge fund financed public positions with leverage subject to margin calls today.

When collateral values fell, lenders did not need to wait for the AI thesis to resolve. They could demand cash or seize positions, forcing the portfolio to crystallize losses and transferring much of it to Citadel.

Aschenbrenner’s reported $400 million private investment days later is consistent with separating those two judgments: remain highly bullish on AI, but shift toward capital that cannot be called away on a daily mark.
This is classic duration mismatch. A potentially correct ten-year view can still destroy a leveraged fund in ten days if the financing structure cannot survive the path.

preschool.title: The Consulting Club That Paid in Parties
preschool.lesson: A group can make money from people’s work even if the workers are paid in something other than cash.
paragraphs: A Harvard student club did consulting work for big companies.
The companies paid the club, but the student consultants did not get salaries.
Lots of students still wanted to join because the club could help them get fancy jobs later.
And the club threw very fancy parties—including one with snakes.

elementary.title: HUCG’s Big Night (with Snakes)
elementary.lesson: Harvard undergrads in the Harvard Undergraduate Consulting Group did paid consulting for companies but were not paid; the group reported almost $7 million in revenue since 2017 and had $2.7 million in net assets as of June 30, 2025, and used some of that money for lavish parties.
paragraphs: At Harvard there’s a club with a serious name, HUCG, a consulting game.
They took on work for AstraZeneca, Delta, Samsung too — over thirty jobs in a year, the kind grown-ups usually do.
Bloomberg’s Samuel Church found the papers and the files, showing students doing projects that would normally pay adults lots of miles.
Since 2017 the club has brought in nearly seven million bucks, and by June 30, 2025 its net assets stood at $2.7 million — not bad for student lucks.
About 450 hopefuls try each term to get inside — only about ten percent succeed, said Noreen Mohamed, the director’s guide.
The application mimics the pros: a written form, a first interview, a mock case study and a final show — a pathway that trains you to land a six-figure job one day, or so.
But here’s the odd and slightly silly, yet true, part of this book: HUCG doesn’t pay the students a salary for the work they took.
Instead the club throws parties on a very grand scale — an estate in Newport, food choices like sirloin or duck on the plate you hail.
There were bars that were open, a fire pit, bouquet-making with flair, and pythons for pictures wrapped around a neck or arm with daring air.

To be clear: Harvard students did paid consulting for big clients, the club reported almost $7 million since 2017 and net assets of $2.7 million as of June 30, 2025, but members did not receive salaries and the organization spent money on lavish events.

What happened? HUCG contracted with companies (AstraZeneca, Delta Air Lines, Samsung Electronics) and generated nearly $7 million in revenue since 2017, with $2.7 million in net assets as of June 30, 2025; students were unpaid and funds were used for large social events including a Newport estate party with multi-course meals and a reptile petting zoo.

middle.title: The $0-Salary Consulting Firm
middle.lesson: Labor can be compensated through credentials, networks and future career options, letting prestigious organizations capture revenue while paying little current cash compensation.
paragraphs: Harvard Undergraduate Consulting Group performs real projects for major corporations, including AstraZeneca, Delta and Samsung. Public filings show almost $7 million of revenue since 2017 and more than $2.7 million of net assets as of mid-2025.

Yet the student consultants are unpaid. Economically, the club can do this because membership itself is scarce and valuable: hundreds apply, about 10% are admitted, and the experience closely imitates the recruiting process for lucrative professional consulting jobs.

The students are therefore receiving non-cash compensation—prestige, training, networking and a credential that may improve future earnings. The club retains cash that a normal consultancy would spend on junior salaries.

Some of that surplus funds unusually lavish social events, including a Newport party with an open bar, dinner and a reptile petting zoo. The joke writes itself: a consulting firm discovered that its labor force may accept pythons instead of payroll.

high.title: Prestige as Compensation
high.lesson: When a credential has enough option value, workers may rationally accept low current wages, allowing an institution to monetize labor while transferring compensation into future career prospects.
paragraphs: HUCG resembles a consulting firm on the revenue side and a selective student organization on the labor-cost side. It has served large corporate clients and accumulated millions in revenue and net assets while paying its student consultants no salary.

The apparent arbitrage depends on prestige. Admission is competitive, the work imitates professional consulting, and membership can signal ability to employers offering six-figure starting compensation. Students may therefore treat unpaid project work as an investment in human capital and career option value.

That does not mean the labor is economically free. The cost is borne by students in time and foregone alternatives, while the club captures the cash revenue. The unusual institutional setting simply converts compensation from wages into credentials, networks, training and social consumption.

The lavish parties—including a Newport event with a reptile petting zoo—make the surplus visible. A conventional firm would distribute more of that value as salary; HUCG can distribute some of it as status and snakes because demand for membership remains extremely high.
